entities.name: Kennedy Space Center
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The John F. Kennedy Space Center (KSC), located on Merritt Island, Florida, is NASA's primary launch center for American human spaceflight and one of ten NASA field centers. Since 1968, KSC has been the operational hub from which every US human spaceflight mission has departed — from Apollo 11's Moon landing (1969) through the Space Shuttle program (1981–2011) to the commercial crew missions of the 2020s.

KSC was established in 1962 to support the Apollo program, President Kennedy's commitment to land Americans on the Moon before 1970. Its iconic Launch Complex 39 — originally built for Saturn V rockets — hosted every Apollo lunar mission, including the historic Apollo 11 launch on July 16, 1969. The same launch pads were later adapted for the Space Shuttle and subsequently for commercial rockets including SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy.

Beyond its role as a launch facility, KSC represents the institutional anchor of American space exploration ambition. The Saturn V rocket (363 feet tall, 6.5 million pounds of thrust) assembled in KSC's Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB) remains the most powerful rocket ever flown. The Space Shuttle's final launch from KSC in 2011 marked the end of an era, but the center's transformation into a multi-tenant spaceport — hosting NASA's Artemis Moon program and commercial operators SpaceX, Boeing, and United Launch Alliance — points toward its continued centrality in the next era of exploration.
